extracted.intended_audience: 17th-century natural philosophers, physicians, anatomists, and microscopists (readers of Philosophical Transactions)
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and interpreting microscopic observations and clinical/anatomical case reports: methods for specimen observation, cautious inference, differential diagnosis between pregnancy and dropsy, and completeness of autopsy description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated and comparative observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm initial microscopic impressions by observing multiple specimens and repeating observations (e.g. 'I have several times endeavoured to observe the parts of a bone... at first I imagined I saw ... but I have not found it since in any other bone').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on a single observation. Compare across specimens (different bones, teeth, species) and repeat examinations to distinguish artifact from real structure. Report when an observation was not replicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer physical properties from dynamic behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Use observable dynamics (settling, motion) to infer physical properties: 'The small red globules in the blood ... are heavier than the crystalline liquor, because, soon after the blood is let out of the veins, those globules gradually subside towards the bottom.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record observable behaviours (e.g., subsiding, effervescence, motion) and link them to inferred properties such as density or interaction with medium, explaining the causal reasoning used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantification by proportional reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide quantitative estimates and justify seemingly incredible measurements by mathematical proportion: 'The red globules of the blood I reckon to be 25,000 times smaller than a grain of sand ... spheres being in a triplicate proportion to their diameters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible give size estimates or ratios and explain the geometric or mathematical basis for those estimates so readers can assess plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed specimen preparation and observation technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe how specimens were prepared and observed (severing filaments, transverse cuts, exposing to microscope, observing under wind): e.g. 'I severed these filaments ... and found the single ones so fine ... exposed them to my microscope' and observing blood blown about in wind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report how samples were handled (cuts, separation), the viewing conditions (drying, exposure to air/wind), and any manipulations that revealed structure or motion. Such methodological detail supports reproducibility and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish observation from conjecture (qualified claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark degrees of confidence and separate conjecture from observed fact: uses of phrases like 'I fancy', 'I have no doubt', 'these yet are but our conjectures and suspicions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about which statements are direct observations, which are inferences, and which are hypotheses. Use qualifying language and note what needs further confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use environmental variation to reveal phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Alter environmental conditions to reveal dynamics (e.g., observing blood globules moved by wind to see rotation): 'going into the open air in high wind, I saw ... the red globules blown about ... as if each globule had yet a second motion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentionally vary viewing conditions (airflow, light, temperature) to test and reveal particle behaviour; report the conditions that produced notable effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential diagnostic criteria for pregnancy vs. dropsy
rubrics_metrics.description: Clinical features used to distinguish pregnancy from ascitic dropsy: presence of regular menstruation, absence of hydropical symptoms (headache, sleepiness, breathing difficulty, thirst), a tumour not prominent or roundish (not typical of pregnancy), and urine not typical of childbearing women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering pregnancy vs. dropsy, gather systemic signs (menstrual history, general health), examine tumor shape and consistency, and inspect urine characteristics; lack of expected pregnancy signs should prompt further investigation (e.g., imaging or tapping where available).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic tests and therapeutic trials as diagnostic information
rubrics_metrics.description: Therapeutic interventions and their effects can inform diagnosis (e.g., use of medicines to make patient void abundance of water which did not reduce the belly, informing diagnosis that the tumor was contained by a membrane).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record treatments attempted and their outcomes; unexpected persistence of a condition after expected response to therapy should lead to reconsideration of diagnosis and further diagnostic steps (e.g., exploratory incision/autopsy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough autopsy/investigation and reporting of internal anatomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct comprehensive internal examination and record presence/absence and state of organs and membranes (e.g., finding peritonaeum turned into a bag, absence or decay of liver, mesentery, pancreas, spleen, kidneys).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In post-mortem reports, systematically inspect and report membranes, visceral organs, and any unusual structural changes; timely incisions may prevent decay and preserve diagnostic information. Note how unexpected findings explain clinical course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document anatomical situs and variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Record positions of major organs and vessels and note any inversions or anomalies (example: inverted order of bowels, heart cone on right side, liver on left, vena cava position).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When anatomical variations are found, document them in detail (positions of heart, liver, spleen, major arteries/veins, ducts, nerves) and comment on any observed clinical consequences or lack thereof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial criterion for educational/practical texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend didactic works that 'omit what is useless and pedantic, and comprehending what is indeed sober and necessary to direct our reason in all sorts of ingenious and useful sciences.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or produce instructional texts by prioritizing essential, practical reasoning tools and removing pedantry; prefer concise, applicable exposition for students and practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward secret remedies and requirement for verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat secret recipes and claimed medicines cautiously ('you may use your own liberty in suspecting the receipts that go about of it ... my justice to the communicator ... made me take that care to conceal some circumstances'), and favor verification by trials and guarded publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of ambiguous names and secret formulations; seek independent trials and reproducible preparation methods before recommending a remedy. When secrecy prevents full disclosure, note limits on reproducibility and trust.
